title: Compact integration onramp — seedling
content:
TL;DR:
Small experiment idea for a low-friction integration onramp for third-party tools and partner plugins. Goal: let customers wire a lightweight adapter (~15m) that exposes data to hosted Redwood endpoints without full Private deployment or Dedicated contracts. Focus on fast time-to-first-request, clear billing attribution, and minimal surface for security review.

Context / problem:
- Customers want to connect common tools (ticketing, CRM, docs storage, analytics) to Redwood features quickly.
- Full Private or Dedicated is heavy: infra, SSO, legal review.
- Today we have SDK + integration guides, but adoption is low because: sensitive security checklists, unclear cost split, and onboarding friction (networking + schema mapping).
- Opportunity: a 'Compact Onramp' that lives in hosted mode but isolates partner adapters with limited scopes and clear runtime limits.

Proposed product (seedling): Compact Integration Adapter (CIA)
- A tiny, hostable adapter pattern + template repo + one-click register flow in Console.
- Runs as a short-lived, Redwood-managed sidecar (sandbox) for partner connectors — not full customer-managed infra.
- Characteristics: scoped API keys, per-integration tokenization, ephemeral credential exchange, default quotas and latency SLOs.
- Billing: usage flows through customer's org but with an attribution tag for partner/adapter.

User personas / success criteria:
- PM or engineer at a mid-market SaaS: can connect Zendesk/Docs in <1 hour and test LLM features end-to-end.
- Solutions engineer: can template a partner adapter and hand to customer with no more than 2 support touchpoints.
- Security reviewer: can read a manifest + auto-generated security posture report and greenlight 80% of adapters without manual code review.

Core flows (happy path):
1) Quickstart: Console -> Integrations -> New Adapter -> choose template (Zendesk/GoogleDrive/Slack).
2) Scaffold: console creates adapter instance with minimal config and shows code snippet to run locally or accept Redwood-managed runtime.
3) Credential exchange: customer pastes API token into Console or triggers OAuth flow; Redwood issues ephemeral adapter token.
4) Test harness: one-click sample prompt + replay UI to validate responses; latency and cost estimate shown.
5) Go live: enable for routes or specific model IDs, set soft quotas.

User stories (examples):
- As a PM, I want to connect a ticketing system so the assistant can fetch recent tickets for context, without provisioning my infra.
- As an SE, I want a template that transforms a vendor API into a minimal schema (id, text, timestamp) so I can reuse it across customers.
- As a security reviewer, I want an automated manifest that lists scopes and data flows so I can do a scoped review in <1 day.

MVP acceptance criteria:
- Template repo with 3 adapters (Zendesk, Google Drive, S3-like object store).
- Console flow to register an adapter and run a test prompt in the hosted runtime.
- Ephemeral adapter tokens with TTL and auditing (logs show adapter activity).
- Basic cost attribution tag visible in billing console (per-adapter).
- Privacy filter: default redaction pipeline for PII extraction (configurable).

Metrics to watch (first 90 days):
- Time-to-first-successful-request (target <30m for 50% of signups).
- Adapter activation rate (template -> active, target 25%).
- SE touchpoints per adapter (target <=2).
- Error rate (adapter-side errors/exceptions, target <3%).
- Billing leakage / misattribution incidents (target 0).

Architecture / tech notes (brain dump):
- Adapter template = small Node/Python shim with defined contract: fetch(), normalize(), auth().
- Runtime modes: Local (developer runs), Redwood-managed sandbox (we run ephemeral container), Customer-managed (future).
- Security: manifest.yaml with declared scopes, dependency SBOM scanned on registration, runtime sandboxing, rate limits.
- Observability: instrument adapter events into existing Console traces; lightweight replay for debugging.
- KV cache: small prefix cache per adapter to avoid repeated fetches; TTL defaults and configurable.

Edge cases & risks:
- Adapter does heavy compute (e.g., local transform) -> need CPU cap and quick kill policy.
- Data exfiltration risk if adapter fetches PII -> default redaction + allowlist for fields.
- Partner support burden if too many templates -> create a review + deprecate policy.
- Billing ambiguity when adapter used across routes & orgs; ensure unique attribution key for every adapter instance.

Compliance notes:
- For EU customers, adapter runtime must accept customer data residency flag; avoid running adapter in non-compliant regions.
- KMS/HSM: do not embed secrets in plain text; use Redwood secret store and rotate ephemeral tokens.

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (internal): build templates + Console flow for internal SEs + 2 pilot accounts. Duration 6 weeks.
- Phase 1 (beta): 10 customers, limit to predefined templates, monitor metrics + SE overhead. Duration 8 weeks.
- Phase 2 (public): enable self-serve, add marketplace UX and partner onboarding docs.

Operational playbook (quick notes):
- Failure mode: adapter error -> automatic fallback to degraded assistant answer (without external context) + notify owning team + ticket created in INTEG queue.
- Abuse detection: rate anomalies + unusual fetch patterns -> auto-disable adapter and require human review.

Open questions / TODOs (notes to self):
- Q: Should adapter runtime be multi-tenant on the same sandbox or 1:1? Tradeoffs: cost vs isolation.
- Q: How granular should billing attribution be? Per-request tag vs per-session.
- Q: What's the minimum manifest we can ask partners to fill out to satisfy legal?
- TODO: prototype Zendesk template (quick map of fields) -> assign to Mika.
- TODO: ping SRE about container TTL and coldstart warmers (Noah).
- TODO: sketch Console mockups for register flow (low fidelity).

Notes on partner UX (raw):
- Make OAuth first-class where possible; fallback to API token but encourage short-lived tokens.
- Show live cost estimate by sampling 10 requests and extrapolating tokens used. That reduces surprise.
- Offer a 'read-only' knob that limits adapters to non-destructive calls.

Hypotheses to validate:
- H1: Reducing infra weight will increase adoption of integrations by PMs (measurable via activation rate).
- H2: Automated manifest + SBOM will reduce security review time by 60%.
- H3: Showing upfront cost estimate reduces churn/abandonment in onboarding flow.

Next actions (immediate):
- Draft quick Zendesk adapter: minimal schema + sample code (target 3 working endpoints).
- Create Console register flow wireframe (1 page) and share with Talia for UX review.
- Set up a pilot tracker board (JIRA: INTEG-212) and add tasks for security gating.

Random scribbles / heuristics:
- "3-click rule" for onboarding: template -> connect creds -> try prompt. If >3 clicks, iterate.
- Default quotas: 10k tokens/day per adapter during beta.
- Use a single attribution header: X-Redwood-Adapter: <org>-<adapter-id> for billing pipes.

Slack trails / links to copy into PRD:
- #product-infra (for rollout comms)
- #security-reviews (for manifest expectations)
- Confluence: /display/INTEG/Compact+Onramp (stub, will create)

My gut: small, iterative experiment with a few high-value templates will show traction. Keep the surface small, make it reversible (easy to disable/remove adapter instances), and instrument everything from the start so we can answer "did this reduce time-to-onboard" quickly.

— ashley
